dhp400.text:
Not irritable or pretentious,
dutiful in precepts and observances,
tamed, bearing their final body:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp400.title: dhp400

dhp401.text:
Like water from a lotus leaf,
like a mustard seed off the point of a pin,
sensual pleasures slip off them:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp401.title: dhp401

dhp402.text:
They understand for themselves
the end of suffering in this life;
with burden put down, detached:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp402.title: dhp402

dhp403.text:
Deep in wisdom, intelligent,
expert in the path and what is not the path;
arrived at the highest goal:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp403.title: dhp403

dhp404.text:
Mixing with neither
householders nor the homeless;
a migrant with no bastion, few in wishes:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp404.title: dhp404

dhp405.text:
They’ve laid aside violence
against creatures firm and frail;
not killing or making others kill:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp405.title: dhp405

dhp406.text:
Not fighting among those who fight,
quenched among those who have taken up arms,
not grasping among those who grasp:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp406.title: dhp406

dhp407.text:
They’ve discarded greed and hate,
along with conceit and contempt,
like a mustard seed off the point of a pin:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp407.title: dhp407

dhp408.text:
The words they utter
are polished, informative, and true,
and don’t offend anyone:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp408.title: dhp408

dhp409.text:
They don’t steal anything in the world,
long or short,
tiny or huge, beautiful or ugly:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp409.title: dhp409

dhp410.text:
They have no hope
in this world or the next;
with no need for hope, detached:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp410.title: dhp410

dhp411.text:
They have no clinging,
knowledge has freed them of indecision,
they’ve arrived at the objective, freedom from death:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp411.title: dhp411

dhp412.text:
They’ve escaped the chain
of both good and bad deeds;
sorrowless, stainless, pure:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp412.title: dhp412

dhp413.text:
Pure as the spotless moon,
clear and unclouded,
they’ve ended relish for rebirth:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp413.title: dhp413

dhp414.text:
They’ve got past this grueling swamp
of delusion, transmigration.
Meditating in stillness, free of indecision,
they have crossed over to the far shore.
They’re quenched by not grasping:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp414.title: dhp414

dhp415.text:
They’ve given up sensual pleasures,
and have gone forth from lay life;
they’ve ended rebirth in the sensual realm:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp415.title: dhp415

dhp417.text:
They’ve thrown off the human yoke,
and slipped out of the heavenly yoke;
unyoked from all yokes:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp417.title: dhp417

dhp418.text:
Giving up desire and discontent,
they’re cooled and free of attachments;
a hero, master of the whole world:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp418.title: dhp418

dhp419.text:
They know the passing away
and rebirth of all beings;
unattached, holy, awakened:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp419.title: dhp419

dhp420.text:
Gods, centaurs, and humans
don’t know their destiny;
the perfected ones with defilements ended:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp420.title: dhp420

dhp421.text:
They have nothing before or after,
or even in between.
Having nothing, taking nothing:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp421.title: dhp421

dhp422.text:
Captain of the herd, excellent hero,
great seer and victor;
unstirred, washed, awakened:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp422.title: dhp422

dhp423.text:
One who knows their past lives,
sees heaven and places of loss,
and has attained the end of rebirth;
a sage of perfect insight
at the summit of spiritual perfection:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
dhp423.title: dhp423

dhp44.text:
Who bestirs this earth,
and the Yama realm with its gods?
Who sets out the well-taught word of truth,
as an expert a flower?
dhp44.title: 4. Flowers

dhp46.text:
Knowing this body’s like foam,
realizing it’s all just a mirage,
and cutting off Māra’s blossoming,
vanish from the King of Death.
dhp46.title: dhp46

dhp47.text:
As a mighty flood sweeps off a sleeping village,
death steals away a man
even as he gathers flowers,
his mind caught up in them.
dhp47.title: dhp47

dhp48.text:
The terminator gains control of the man
who has not had his fill of pleasures,
even as he gathers flowers,
his mind caught up in them.
dhp48.title: dhp48

dhp49.text:
A bee takes the nectar
and moves on, doing no damage
to the flower’s beauty and fragrance;
and that’s how a sage should walk in the village.
dhp49.title: dhp49

dhp50.text:
Don’t find fault with others,
with what they’ve done or left undone.
You should only watch yourself,
what you’ve done or left undone.
dhp50.title: dhp50

dhp51.text:
Just like a glorious flower
that’s colorful but lacks fragrance;
eloquent speech is fruitless
for one who does not act on it.
dhp51.title: dhp51

dhp52.text:
Just like a glorious flower
that’s both colorful and fragrant,
eloquent speech is fruitful
for one who acts on it.
dhp52.title: dhp52

dhp53.text:
Just as one would create many garlands
from a heap of flowers,
when a person has come to be born,
they should do many skillful things.
dhp53.title: dhp53

dhp54.title: dhp54

dhp55.text:
Among all the fragrances—
sandalwood or pinwheel
or lotus or jasmine—
the fragrance of virtue is supreme.
dhp55.title: dhp55

dhp56.text:
Faint is the fragrance
of sandal or pinwheel;
but the fragrance of the virtuous
floats to the highest gods.
dhp56.title: dhp56

dhp57.text:
For those accomplished in ethics,
meditating diligently,
freed through the highest knowledge,
Māra cannot find their path.
dhp57.title: dhp57

dhp58.text:
From a heap of trash
discarded on the highway,
a lotus might blossom,
fragrant and delightful.
dhp58.title: dhp58

dhp59.text:
So too, among those thought of as trash,
a disciple of the perfect Buddha
outshines with their wisdom
the blind ordinary folk.
dhp59.title: dhp59

dhp60.title: 5. The Fool

dhp61.text:
If while wandering you find no partner
equal or better than yourself,
then firmly resolve to wander alone—
there’s no fellowship with fools.
dhp61.title: dhp61

dhp62.text:
“Sons are mine, wealth is mine”—
thus the fool frets.
For even your self is not your own,
let alone your sons or wealth.
dhp62.title: dhp62

dhp63.text:
The fool who thinks they’re a fool
is wise at least to that extent.
But the true fool is said to be one
who imagines that they are wise.
dhp63.title: dhp63

dhp64.text:
Though a fool attends to the wise
even for the rest of their life,
they still don’t understand the teaching,
like a spoon the taste of the soup.
dhp64.title: dhp64

dhp65.text:
If a clever person attends to the wise
even just for an hour or so,
they swiftly understand the teaching,
like a tongue the taste of the soup.
dhp65.title: dhp65

dhp66.text:
Fools and simpletons behave
like their own worst enemies,
doing wicked deeds
that ripen as bitter fruit.
dhp66.title: dhp66

dhp67.text:
It’s not good to do a deed
that plagues you later on,
for which you weep and wail,
as its effect stays with you.
dhp67.title: dhp67

dhp68.text:
It is good to do a deed
that doesn’t plague you later on,
that gladdens and cheers,
as its effect stays with you.
dhp68.title: dhp68

dhp69.text:
The fool imagines that evil is sweet,
so long as it has not yet ripened.
But as soon as that evil ripens,
they fall into suffering.
dhp69.title: dhp69

dhp70.text:
Month after month a fool may eat
food from a grass-blade’s tip;
but they’ll never be worth a sixteenth part
of one who has appraised the teaching.
dhp70.title: dhp70

dhp71.text:
For a wicked deed that has been done
does not curdle quickly like milk.
Smoldering, it follows the fool,
like a fire smothered over with ash.
dhp71.title: dhp71

dhp72.text:
Whatever fame a fool may get,
it only gives rise to harm.
Whatever good features they have it ruins,
and blows their head into bits.
dhp72.title: dhp72

dhp73.text:
They’d seek the esteem that they lack,
and status among the mendicants;
authority over monasteries,
and honor among other families.
dhp73.title: dhp73

dhp74.text:
“Let both layfolk and renunciants think
the work was done by me alone.
In anything at all that’s to be done,
let them fall under my sway alone.”
So thinks the fool,
their greed and pride only growing.
dhp74.title: dhp74

dhp75.text:
For the means to profit and the path to quenching
are two quite different things.
A mendicant disciple of the Buddha,
understanding what this really means,
would never delight in honors,
but rather would foster seclusion.
dhp75.title: dhp75

dhp76.text:
Regard one who sees your faults
as a guide to a hidden treasure.
Stay close to one so intelligent and astute
who curbs you when you need it.
Sticking close to such an impartial person,
things get better, not worse.
dhp76.title: 6. The Astute

dhp77.title: dhp77

dhp78.text:
Don’t mix with bad friends,
nor with the worst of men.
Mix with spiritual friends,
and with the best of men.
dhp78.title: dhp78

dhp79.text:
Through joy in the teaching you sleep at ease,
with clear and confident heart.
An astute person always delights in the teaching
proclaimed by the Noble One.
dhp79.title: dhp79

dhp80.text:
While irrigators guide water,
fletchers bend arrows straight,
and carpenters bend timber straight,
the astute tame themselves.
dhp80.title: dhp80

dhp81.text:
As the wind cannot stir
a solid mass of rock,
so too blame and praise
do not affect the wise.
dhp81.title: dhp81

dhp82.text:
Like a deep lake,
clear and unclouded,
so clear are the astute
when they hear the teachings.
dhp82.title: dhp82

dhp83.text:
True persons give up everything,
they don’t cajole for the things they desire.
Though touched by sadness or happiness,
the astute appear neither depressed nor elated.
dhp83.title: dhp83

dhp84.title: dhp84

dhp85.text:
Few are those among humans
who cross to the far shore.
The rest just run around
on the near shore.
dhp85.title: dhp85

dhp86.text:
When the teaching is well explained,
the people who practice accordingly
will cross over
Death’s dominion so hard to pass.
dhp86.title: dhp86

dhp87.text:
Rid of dark qualities,
an astute person would develop the bright.
Having left home for homelessness
in seclusion, where joy is hard,
dhp87.title: dhp87

dhp88.text:
they’d long for satisfaction there.
Forsaking sensual pleasures, owning nothing,
an astute person would cleanse themselves
of mental corruptions.
dhp88.title: dhp88

dhp89.text:
And those whose minds are rightly developed
in the awakening factors;
who, letting go of attachments,
delight in not grasping:
with defilements ended, brilliant,
they are quenched in this world.
dhp89.title: dhp89

dhp90.text:
At journey’s end, rid of sorrow;
everywhere free,
all ties given up,
no fever is found in them.
dhp90.title: 7. The Perfected Ones

dhp91.text:
The mindful apply themselves;
they delight in no abode.
Like a swan gone from the marsh,
they leave home after home behind.
dhp91.title: dhp91

dhp92.text:
Those with nothing stored up,
who have understood their food,
whose domain is the liberation
of the signless and the empty:
their path is hard to trace,
like birds in the sky.
dhp92.title: dhp92

dhp93.title: dhp93

dhp94.text:
Whose faculties have become serene,
like horses tamed by a charioteer,
who has abandoned conceit and defilements;
the unaffected one is envied by even the gods.
dhp94.title: dhp94

dhp95.text:
Undisturbed like the earth,
true to their vows, steady as Indra’s pillar,
like a lake clear of mud;
such a one does not transmigrate.
dhp95.title: dhp95

dhp96.text:
Their mind is peaceful,
peaceful are their speech and deeds.
Such a one is at peace,
rightly freed through enlightenment.
dhp96.title: dhp96

dhp97.text:
Lacking faith, a house-breaker,
one who acknowledges nothing,
purged of hope, they’ve wasted their chance:
that is indeed the supreme person!
dhp97.title: dhp97

dhp98.text:
Whether in village or wilderness,
in a valley or the uplands,
wherever the perfected ones live
is a delightful place.
dhp98.title: dhp98

dhp99.text:
Delightful are the wildernesses
where no people delight.
Those free of greed will delight there,
not those who seek sensual pleasures.
dhp99.title: dhp99

thag1.100.text:
Accomplished in the four right efforts,
mindfulness meditation is your range;
festooned with the flowers of liberation,
undefiled, you’ll be fully quenched.
thag1.100.title: Devasabha (2nd)

thag1.101.text:
He’s given up the household life, <j>but is far from perfect.
Living for his belly, lazy, <j>he uses his snout as a plow,
like a great hog stuffed with grain.
That dullard is reborn again and again.
thag1.101.title: Belaṭṭhānika

thag1.102.text:
Deceived by conceit,
defiled among conditions,
oppressed by gain and loss,
they don’t reach immersion.
thag1.102.title: Setuccha

thag1.103.text:
I have no need of this—
I’m happy and satisfied with the sweet teaching.
I’ve drunk the best, the supreme nectar:
I won’t go near poison.
thag1.103.title: Bandhura

thag1.104.text:
Hey! My body is light,
full of so much rapture and happiness.
My body feels like it’s floating,
like cotton in a gale.
thag1.104.title: Khitaka

thag1.105.text:
Dissatisfied, one should not stay;
and even if happy, one should leave.
One who sees clearly wouldn’t stay
in a place that was not conducive to the goal.
thag1.105.title: Malitavambha

thag1.106.text:
Though the meaning has a hundred facets,
and bears a hundred characteristics,
the simpleton sees only one factor,
while the sage sees a hundred.
thag1.106.title: Suhemanta

thag1.107.text:
After investigating, I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.107.title: Dhammasava

thag1.109.text:
Even on retreat he doesn’t heed the counsel
of the one with supreme compassion for his welfare.
He lives with unrestrained faculties,
like a young deer in the woods.
thag1.109.title: Saṅgharakkhita

thag1.10.text:
A knowledge master, peaceful and self-controlled,
is rid of concern for this world and the world beyond.
Unsullied in the midst of all things,
they’d know the arising and passing of the world.
thag1.10.title: Puṇṇamāsa (1st)

thag1.110.text:
The trees on the mountain tops have grown tall,
freshly sprinkled by towering clouds.
For Usabha, who loves seclusion, <j>and who thinks only of wilderness,
goodness flourishes more and more.
thag1.110.title: Usabha (1st)

thag1.111.text:
Going forth is hard; living at home is hard;
Dhamma is profound; money is hard to come by.
Getting by is difficult for we <j>who accept whatever comes,
so we should always think about impermanence.
thag1.111.title: Jenta

thag1.112.text:
I am a master of the three knowledges, <j>I’m a great meditator,
an expert in serenity of heart.
I’ve realized my heart’s goal
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.112.title: Vacchagotta

thag1.113.text:
The water’s clear and the rocks are broad,
monkeys and deer are all around;
festooned with dewy moss,
these rocky crags delight me!
thag1.113.title: Vanavaccha (2nd)

thag1.114.text:
Your body is uncomfortably heavy,
and life is running out;
greedy for physical pleasure,
how can you find happiness as an ascetic?
thag1.114.title: Adhimutta (1st)

thag1.115.text:
By Mount Nesādaka,
with its famous covering
of abundant shrubs and trees,
you’re found deficient.
thag1.115.title: Mahānāma

thag1.116.text:
I’ve given up the six spheres of sense-contact,
my sense doors are guarded and well restrained;
I’ve ejected the root of gloom
and attained the ending of defilements.
thag1.116.title: Pārāsariya (1st)

thag1.117.text:
I’m well-anointed and well-dressed,
adorned with all my jewelry.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.117.title: Yasa

thag1.118.text:
Old age falls like a curse;
it’s the same body, but it seems like someone else’s.
I remember myself as if I were someone else,
but I’m still the same, I haven’t been away.
thag1.118.title: Kimbila (1st)

thag1.119.text:
You’ve left for the jungle, the root of a tree,
having laid extinguishment in your heart.
Meditate, Gotama, don’t be negligent!
What use is this hullabaloo to you?
thag1.119.title: Vajjiputta (2nd)

thag1.120.text:
The five aggregates are fully understood,
they remain, but their root is cut.
I have reached the end of suffering
and attained the ending of defilements.
thag1.120.title: Isidatta

thag1.12.text:
Empowered by wisdom, <j>with precepts and observances intact,
serene, loving absorption, mindful,
eating just the needed food,
one should await one’s time here, free of desire.
thag1.12.title: Mahāvaccha

thag1.13.text:
Glistening, they look like blue stormclouds,
with waters cool and streams so clear,
and covered all in ladybugs:
these rocky crags delight me!
thag1.13.title: Vanavaccha (1st)

thag1.14.text:
My mentor said to me:
“Let’s leave here, Sīvaka.”
My body lives in the village,
but my mind has gone to the wilderness.
I go there even when lying down—
you can’t chain those who know.
thag1.14.title: The Novice Sivaka

thag1.16.text:
Just as a fine thoroughbred
proceeds with ease,
tail and mane flying in the wind;
so my days and nights
proceed with ease,
full of joy not of the flesh.
thag1.16.title: Belaṭṭhasīsa

thag1.18.text:
There was an heir of the Buddha,
a monk in Bhesakaḷā forest,
who suffused the entire earth
with the perception of bones.
I think he will quickly
get rid of sensual desire.
thag1.18.title: Sigāla’s Father

thag1.1.text:
Like the lions of mighty fang
who roar in mountain caves—
hear now from those who’ve practiced well
their own verses about themselves.
thag1.1.title: Subhūti

thag1.20.text:
I do not fear death;
nor do I long for life.
I’ll lay down this body,
aware and mindful.
thag1.20.title: Ajita

thag1.21.text:
I’m not afraid of fear,
for our teacher is expert in freedom from death.
Mendicants advance by the path
where no fear remains.
thag1.21.title: Nigrodha

thag1.22.text:
Crested peacocks with beautiful blue necks
cry out in Karaṁvī.
Stirred by a cool breeze,
they wake the sleeper to practice absorption.
thag1.22.title: Cittaka

thag1.23.text:
I’ll eat honey and milk-rice
in Veḷugumba.
And then, dexterously probing
the rise and fall of the aggregates,
I’ll return to my forest hill
and foster seclusion.
thag1.23.title: Gosāla

thag1.24.text:
See the excellence of the teaching!
Just one rainy season after I went forth,
I attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.24.title: Sugandha

thag1.25.text:
Dark One, after attacking such a monk—
one who has arrived at the fruit,
and whose mind is always full of light—
you’ll fall into suffering.
thag1.25.title: Nandiya

thag1.26.text:
Having heard the fine words
of the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun,
I penetrated the subtle truth,
like a hair-tip with an arrow.
thag1.26.title: Abhaya

thag1.27.text:
With my chest I’ll thrust aside
the grasses, vines, canes,
the vetiver, rushes and reeds,
and foster seclusion.
thag1.27.title: Lomasakaṅgiya

thag1.28.text:
Aren’t you obsessed with clothes?
Don’t you just love jewelry?
Is it not you—and no one else—
who spreads the scent of virtue?
thag1.28.title: Jambugāmikaputta

thag1.29.text:
Straighten yourself,
like a fletcher an arrow.
When your mind is upright, Hārita,
break ignorance to bits!
thag1.29.title: Hārita (1st)

thag1.2.text:
Calm and still,
thoughtful in counsel, not restless—
he shakes off bad qualities
as the gale shakes leaves off a tree.
thag1.2.title: Mahākoṭṭhita

thag1.30.text:
When I was ill in the past,
mindfulness arose in me.
Now I am ill once more—
it’s time for me to be heedful.
thag1.30.title: Uttiya (1st)

thag1.31.text:
Pestered by flies and mosquitoes
in the wilds, the formidable forest,
one should mindfully endure,
like an elephant at the head of the battle.
thag1.31.title: Gahvaratīriya

thag1.32.text:
I’ll swap old age for the unaging,
burning for quenching—
the ultimate peace,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
thag1.32.title: Suppiya

thag1.33.text:
Just as a mother would be good
to her beloved only child;
so, to creatures all and everywhere,
let one be good.
thag1.33.title: Sopāka (1st)

thag1.34.text:
It’s always better for a smart person
to avoid sharing a seat with such women.
I went from the village to the wilderness;
from there I entered a house.
Though I was there to be fed,
I got up and left without taking leave.
thag1.34.title: Posiya

thag1.35.text:
Seeking happiness, they find it through this practice.
They get a good reputation and grow in fame,
those who develop the direct route:
the noble eightfold path to realize freedom from death.
thag1.35.title: Sāmaññakāni

thag1.36.text:
Learning is good, living well is good,
the life without abode is always good.
Questions on the meaning, actions that are skillful:
this is the ascetic life for one who has nothing.
thag1.36.title: Kumāputta

thag1.37.text:
Some travel to different countries,
wandering undisciplined.
If they lose their meditation,
what will such rotten conduct achieve?
So you should dispel aggression,
practicing absorption undistracted.
thag1.37.title: Kumāputtasahāyaka

thag1.38.text:
His psychic power made the Sarabhū River stand still;
Gavampati is unbound and unperturbed.
The gods bow to that great sage, <j>who has slipped all chains,
and gone beyond rebirth.
thag1.38.title: Gavampati

thag1.39.text:
Like they’re struck by a sword,
like their head was on fire,
a mendicant should wander mindful
to give up sensual desire.
thag1.39.title: Tissa (1st)

thag1.3.text:
See this wisdom of the Realized Ones!
Like a fire blazing in the night,
giving light, giving vision,
they dispel the doubt of those who’ve come.
thag1.3.title: Revata the Doubter

thag1.41.text:
Lightning flashes down
on the cleft of Vebhāra and Paṇḍava.
But in the mountain cleft he is absorbed in jhāna—
the son of the Buddha, inimitable and unaffected.
thag1.41.title: Sirivaḍḍha

thag1.42.text:
Cālā, Upacālā, Sīsupacālā—
meditate mindfully!
I’ve come to you like a hair-splitter.
thag1.42.title: Revata of the Acacia Wood

thag1.43.text:
Well freed! Well freed!
I’m very well freed from three crooked things:
my sickles, my ploughs,
and my little hoes.
Even if they were here, right here—
I’d be done with them, done!
Practice absorption Sumaṅgala! <j>Practice absorption Sumaṅgala!
Stay heedful, Sumaṅgala!
thag1.43.title: Sumaṅgala

thag1.44.text:
Mum, they weep for the dead,
or for one who’s alive but missing.
I’m alive and you can see me,
so mum, why do you weep for me?
thag1.44.title: Sānu

thag1.45.text:
Though a fine thoroughbred may stumble,
it soon stands firm again.
Even so is one accomplished in vision,
a disciple of the Buddha.
thag1.45.title: Ramaṇīyavihārin

thag1.46.text:
I went forth out of faith
from the lay life to homelessness.
My mindfulness and wisdom have grown,
my mind is serene.
Make whatever illusions you want,
it doesn’t bother me.
thag1.46.title: Samiddhi

thag1.47.text:
Homage to you, O Buddha, O hero,
freed in every way!
Meditating in the fruits of your practice,
I live without defilements.
thag1.47.title: Ujjaya

thag1.48.text:
Since I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness,
I’ve not been aware of any thought
that is ignoble and hateful.
thag1.48.title: Sañjaya

thag1.49.text:
Even with all the sounds,
the chirping and cheeping of the birds,
my mind doesn’t flounder,
for I’m devoted to oneness.
thag1.49.title: Rāmaṇeyyaka

thag1.4.text:
Associate only with the virtuous,
the astute ones who see the goal.
The attentive ones, diligent and clear-seeing,
realize the goal
so great and profound,
hard to see, subtle, and very fine.
thag1.4.title: Puṇṇa (1st)

thag1.50.text:
The celestial lake Dharaṇī pours, <j>the heavenly gale blows,
and lightning flashes across the sky!
But my thoughts are stilled,
my mind is serene.
thag1.50.title: Vimala (1st)

thag1.51.text:
The heavens rain like a sweet song;
my hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind.
My mind is serene:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.
thag1.51.title: Godhika

thag1.55.text:
I plunged into the Añjana wood
and made a hut to live in.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.55.title: Añjanavaniya

thag1.56.text:
“Who is in this hut?” “A monk is in this hut,
free of lust, his mind serene.
Reverend, you should know this:
your hut wasn’t built in vain.”
thag1.56.title: Kuṭivihārin (1st)

thag1.57.text:
This was your old hut,
but you still want a new hut.
Let go of hope for a hut, monk!
A new hut will only bring more suffering.
thag1.57.title: Kuṭivihārin (2nd)

thag1.58.text:
My hut is pleasing, delightful,
a gift given in faith.
I’ve no need of girls:
go, ladies, to those in need!
thag1.58.title: Ramaṇīyakuṭika

thag1.59.text:
I went forth out of faith
and built a hut in the wilderness.
I’m heedful, ardent,
aware, and mindful.
thag1.59.title: Kosalavihārin

thag1.5.title: Dabba

thag1.60.text:
My wishes—the purpose I had
for entering this hut—came true.
Seeking knowledge and liberation,
I gave up the tendency to conceit.
thag1.60.title: Sīvali

thag1.61.text:
One who sees
sees those who see and those who don’t.
One who doesn’t see
sees neither.
thag1.61.title: Vappa

thag1.62.text:
We dwell alone in the wilderness,
like a log dumped in a forest.
Lots of people are jealous of me,
as beings in hell are of one going to heaven.
thag1.62.title: Vajjiputta (1st)

thag1.63.text:
They fall, collapsed and fallen;
greedy, they return.
The work is done, the joyful is enjoyed,
happiness is found through happiness.
thag1.63.title: Pakkha

thag1.64.text:
I arose from the one named after a tree;
I was born of the one whose banner shines.
The banner killer has destroyed the great banner,
by means of the banner itself.
thag1.64.title: Vimalakoṇḍañña

thag1.65.text:
Vaccha has tossed away
what he built over many years.
Sitting comfortably, uplifted with joy,
he teaches this to householders.
thag1.65.title: Ukkhepakatavaccha

thag1.66.text:
He counseled me, the great hero,
the one who has gone beyond all things.
When I heard his teaching
I stayed close by him, mindful.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thag1.66.title: Meghiya

thag1.67.text:
My defilements have been burnt away <j>by practicing absorption—
rebirth into all states of existence is eradicated,
transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag1.67.title: Ekadhammasavanīya

thag1.69.text:
Hearing the sweet Dhamma taught by the master,
all-knowing, of superb knowledge,
I’ve entered the path to realize freedom from death—
he is the expert on the road to sanctuary from the yoke.
thag1.69.title: Channa

thag1.6.text:
The monk who went to the Cool Grove is solitary,
content and serene,
victorious, with goosebumps vanished,
guarding mindfulness of the body, steadfast.
thag1.6.title: Sītavaniya

thag1.70.text:
Ethical conduct is best in this life,
but one with wisdom is supreme.
Someone with both virtue and wisdom
is victorious among men and gods.
thag1.70.title: Puṇṇa (2nd)

thag1.71.title: Vacchapāla

thag1.72.text:
A young bamboo is hard to extract
when the point is grown and become all woody.
That’s how I feel with the wife <j>who was arranged for me.
Give me permission—now I’ve gone forth.
thag1.72.title: Ātuma

thag1.73.text:
Seeing an old person, and one suffering from disease,
and a corpse come to the end of life,
I went forth, becoming a wanderer,
and giving up the pleasures of the senses.
thag1.73.title: Māṇava

thag1.74.text:
Sensual desire, ill will,
dullness and drowsiness,
restlessness, and doubt
are not found in a monk at all.
thag1.74.title: Suyāmana

thag1.75.text:
Good is the sight of those who’ve practiced well:
doubt is cut off and intelligence grows—
even a fool grows wise!
That’s why it’s good to meet good people.
thag1.75.title: Susārada

thag1.76.title: Piyañjaha

thag1.78.text:
Transmigrating through countless rebirths,
I’ve journeyed without reward.
I’ve suffered, but now
the mass of suffering has fallen away.
thag1.78.title: Meṇḍasira

thag1.79.text:
All my lust is given up,
all my hate is eradicated,
all my delusion is gone:
I’m cooled, quenched.
thag1.79.title: Rakkhita

thag1.7.text:
He has cast aside the army of the King of Death,
as a fragile bridge of reeds by a great flood.
Victorious since his fears have vanished:
tame and steadfast, he has become quenched.
thag1.7.title: Bhalliya

thag1.80.text:
Any deeds I have done,
a little or a lot,
are all completely exhausted:
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag1.80.title: Ugga

thag1.81.text:
Any bad things I’ve done
in previous lives,
are to be experienced right here,
not in any other place.
thag1.81.title: Samitigutta

thag1.82.text:
Go, child, to any place
where there’s plenty of food,
where it’s safe and free of peril—
may you not be overcome by sorrow!
thag1.82.title: Kassapa

thag1.83.text:
Meditate diligently, Sīha,
tireless all day and night.
Develop skillful qualities,
and quickly discard this bag of bones.
thag1.83.title: Sīha

thag1.84.text:
Sleeping all night,
happily socializing by day,
when will the simpleton
make an end of suffering?
thag1.84.title: Nīta

thag1.85.text:
Skilled in the patterns of the mind,
understanding the nectar of seclusion,
practicing absorption, alert, mindful:
such a person would realize pleasure not of the flesh.
thag1.85.title: Sunāga

thag1.86.title: Nāgita

thag1.87.title: Paviṭṭha

thag1.88.text:
I was able to lift myself up
from the water to the shore.
While being swept away by the great flood,
I penetrated the truths.
thag1.88.title: Ajjuna

thag1.89.text:
I’ve crossed the bogs,
I’ve avoided the chasms,
I’m freed from floods and ties,
and I’ve wiped out all conceit.
thag1.89.title: Devasabha (1st)

thag1.90.text:
The five aggregates are fully understood;
they remain, but their root is cut.
Transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag1.90.title: Sāmidatta

thag1.91.text:
What I consumed today is considered better
than delicious grain of a hundred flavors—
the Dhamma taught by the Buddha,
Gotama of infinite vision.
thag1.91.title: Paripuṇṇaka

thag1.93.text:
Sensual pleasures are suffering, Eraka!
Sensual pleasures aren’t happiness, Eraka!
One who enjoys sensual pleasures
enjoys suffering, Eraka!
One who doesn’t enjoy sensual pleasures
doesn’t enjoy suffering, Eraka!
thag1.93.title: Eraka

thag1.94.text:
Homage to that Blessed One,
the glorious Sakyan!
Having reached the best,
he beautifully taught the best teaching.
thag1.94.title: Mettaji

thag1.95.text:
I’m blind, my eyes are ruined,
I’m traveling a desolate road.
Even if I have to crawl I’ll keep going—
though not with wicked companions.
thag1.95.title: Cakkhupāla

thag1.96.text:
I offered a single flower
and then amused myself in heavens
for 800 million years;
with what’s left over I’ve become quenched.
thag1.96.title: Khaṇḍasumana

thag1.97.text:
Giving up a hundred ounces of bronze,
and a hundred grains of gold,
I took a bowl made of clay:
this is my second initiation.
thag1.97.title: Tissa (2nd)

thag1.98.text:
When you see a sight, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.
Your defilements grow,
leading to the root of rebirth.
thag1.98.title: Abhaya

thag1.9.text:
It was welcome, not unwelcome,
the advice I got was good.
Of the well-explained teachings,
I arrived at the best.
thag1.9.title: Pilindavaccha

thag10.1.text:
“The trees are now crimson, venerable sir,
they’ve shed their foliage, and are ready to fruit.
They shine as if aflame;
great hero, this season is full of flavor.
thag10.1.title: Kāḷudāyī

thag10.2.text:
If no one else is found
before or behind,
it’s extremely pleasant
to be dwelling alone in a forest grove.
thag10.2.title: Ekavihāriya

thag10.3.text:
If you’re prepared for the future,
both the good and the bad,
then those, whether enemies or well-wishers,
who examine you for weakness will see none.
thag10.3.title: Mahākappina

thag10.4.text:
My progress was slow,
I was despised in the past.
Even my brother turned me away,
saying, “Go home now.”
thag10.4.title: Cūḷapanthaka

thag10.5.text:
full of pus and blood,
sunk in a toilet-pit,
trickling with fluids,
this rotting body always oozes.
thag10.5.title: Kappa

thag10.6.text:
In order to go on retreat,
a monk should stay in lodgings
that are secluded and quiet,
frequented by beasts of prey.
thag10.6.title: Upasena son of Vaṅgantā

thag10.7.text:
You should understand your own goal,
and consider the dispensation carefully,
as well as what’s appropriate
for one who has entered the ascetic life.
thag10.7.title: Another Gotama

thag11.1.text:
“What good does it do you to be in the grove, my dear?
You’re like a little bird in the monsoon!
The city of Verambhā is nice for you—
seclusion is for meditators.”
thag11.1.title: Saṅkicca

thag12.1.text:
One should train just in ethical conduct,
for in this world, when ethical conduct is
cultivated and well-trained,
it provides all success.
thag12.1.title: Sīlava

thag12.2.text:
I was born in a low-class family.
We were poor, with little to eat.
My job was lowly—
I threw out the old flowers.
thag12.2.title: Sunīta

thag14.2.text:
Just as a fine thoroughbred,
yoked to a carriage, endures the load.
Though oppressed by the heavy burden,
it doesn’t shake off the yoke.
thag14.2.title: Godatta

thag15.1.text:
“My confidence grew
as I heard the teaching, so full of flavor.
Dispassion is what was taught,
without any grasping at all.”
thag15.1.title: Koṇḍañña Who Understood

thag15.2.text:
Awakened as a human being,
self-tamed and immersed in samādhi,
following the spiritual path,
he loves peace of mind.
thag15.2.title: Udāyī

thag16.10.text:
“The behavior of the mendicants
these days seems different
from when the protector of the world,
the best of men, was still here.
thag16.10.title: Pārāsariya (3rd)

thag16.1.text:
I’ve lived the spiritual life well,
and developed the path well, too.
I do not fear death;
it’s like the passing of a disease.
thag16.1.title: Adhimutta (2nd)

thag16.2.text:
“Following what procedure,
what observance, what conduct,
may a person do what they need for themselves,
without harming anyone else?
thag16.2.title: Pārāsariya (2nd)

thag16.3.text:
I was hooked inside,
like a fish gulping bait;
bound like the titan Vepaciti
in Mahinda’s trap.
thag16.3.title: Telakāni

thag16.5.text:
Many feelings grow
arising from sights.
The mind is damaged
by covetousness and cruelty.
Heaping up suffering like this,
you’re said to be far from extinguishment.
thag16.5.title: Māluṅkyaputta (2nd)

thag16.6.text:
“O Blessed One, your body’s perfect,
you’re radiant, handsome, lovely to behold;
golden colored,
with teeth so white; you’re strong.
thag16.6.title: Sela

thag16.7.text:
I rode on an elephant’s neck,
wearing luxurious clothes.
I ate boiled fine rice
with pure meat sauce.
thag16.7.title: Kāḷigodhāputtabhaddiya

thag16.8.text:
“Aṅgulimāla, I have forever stopped—
I’ve laid aside violence toward all creatures.
But you can’t stop yourself <j>from harming living creatures;
that’s why I’ve stopped, but you have not.”
thag16.8.title: Aṅgulimāla

thag16.9.text:
Leaving my mother and father behind,
as well as sisters, kinsmen, and brothers;
having given up the five sensual stimuli,
Anuruddha practices absorption.
thag16.9.title: Anuruddha

thag17.1.text:
“In future times,
what desire and motivation
and behavior will people have?
Please answer my question.”
thag17.1.title: Phussa

thag17.2.text:
“One who’s mindful <j>as per their conduct and mindfulness,
diligent <j>as per their intentions and meditation,
happy inside, serene, solitary, contented:
that is what they call a mendicant.
thag17.2.title: Sāriputta

thag17.3.text:
“The astute would not make friends
with the slanderous or the hateful,
with a miser or a gloater,
for it’s bad to consort with reprobates.
thag17.3.title: Ānanda

thag18.1.text:
“You shouldn’t live for the adulation of a following;
it turns your mind, making it hard to get immersion.
Seeing that popularity is suffering,
you shouldn’t consent to a following.
thag18.1.title: Mahākassapa

thag19.1.text:
Oh, when will I stay in a mountain cave,
alone, with no companion,
discerning all states of existence as impermanent?
This hope of mine, <j>when will it be?
thag19.1.title: Tālapuṭa

thag2.10.text:
First one kills oneself,
then one kills others.
One kills oneself, really dead,
like one who kills birds using a dead bird as a decoy.
A brahmin’s color is not on the outside;
a brahmin is colored on the inside.
Whoever harbors bad deeds
is truly a dark one, Sujampati.
thag2.10.title: Vasabha

thag2.11.title: Mahācunda

thag2.12.text:
People who act harshly—
attacking people,
binding them with rope,
hurting them in all kinds of ways—
they’re treated in the same way;
their deeds don’t vanish.
Whatever deeds a person does,
whether good or bad,
they are the heir to each
and every deed they do.
thag2.12.title: Jotidāsa

thag2.13.text:
The days and nights rush by,
and then life is cut short.
The life of mortals wastes away,
like the water in tiny streams.
But while doing bad deeds
the fool doesn’t realize—
it’ll be bitter later on;
for the result will be bad for them.
thag2.13.title: Heraññakāni

thag2.14.text:
If you’re lost in the middle of a great sea,
and you clamber up on a little log, you’ll sink.
So too, a person who lives well
sinks by relying on a lazy person.
Hence you should avoid such
a lazy person who lacks energy.
thag2.14.title: Somamitta

thag2.15.title: Sabbamitta

thag2.16.title: Mahākāḷa

thag2.17.text:
A shaven one wrapped in the outer robe
gets many enemies
when they receive food and drink,
clothes and bedding.
Knowing this danger,
this great fear in honors,
a mendicant should wander mindful,
with few possessions, not festering.
thag2.17.title: Tissa (3rd)

thag2.18.text:
In the Park of the East-Raftered Hall
the Sakyan friends,
having given up great wealth,
are happy with the scraps in their bowls.
Energetic, resolute,
always staunchly vigorous;
having given up mundane delights,
they enjoy the delights of the Dhamma.
thag2.18.title: Kimbila (2nd)

thag2.19.text:
Because of focusing on the wrong things,
I was addicted to ornamentation.
I was vain, fickle,
racked by desire for pleasures of the senses.
But with the help of the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun, so skilled in means,
I practiced rationally and extracted
attachment to continued existence from my mind.
thag2.19.title: Nanda

thag2.1.text:
No life is permanent,
and no conditions last forever.
The aggregates are reborn
and pass away, again and again.
Knowing this danger,
I have no need for another life.
I’ve escaped all sensual pleasures,
and attained the ending of defilements.
thag2.1.title: Uttara (1st)

thag2.20.text:
If others praise one
who has no immersion,
they praise in vain,
as one has no immersion.
If others criticize one
who does have immersion,
they criticize in vain,
as one does have immersion.
thag2.20.title: Sirima

thag2.21.text:
I’ve fully understood the aggregates;
I’ve eradicated craving;
I’ve developed the factors of awakening,
I’ve attained the ending of defilements.
Having fully understood the aggregates,
having plucked out the weaver of the web,
having developed the factors of awakening,
being undefiled, I will be fully extinguished.
thag2.21.title: Uttara (2nd)

thag2.22.text:
There was a king named Panāda
who had a sacrificial post all golden.
Its height was sixteen times its width,
and the top was a thousandfold.
It had a thousand panels and a hundred ball-caps,
all adorned with banners, and made of sun gold.
There danced the centaurs,
numbering seven times six thousand.
thag2.22.title: Bhaddaji

thag2.23.text:
As a monk, mindful and wise,
empowered and full of energy,
I recollected five hundred eons
in a single night.
Developing the four mindfulness meditations,
the seven factors of awakening, <j>and the eightfold path,
I recollected five hundred eons
in a single night.
thag2.23.title: Sobhita

thag2.24.text:
The duty of one whose energy is strong;
the duty of one who longs to wake up:
that I’ll do, I won’t fail—
see my energy and vigor!
Teach me the path,
the direct route whose objective is freedom from death.
I’ll know it with wisdom,
as the Ganges knows the ocean.
thag2.24.title: Valliya (3rd)

thag2.25.text:
The barber approached
to shave my head.
I picked up a mirror
and examined my body.
My body appeared hollow;
I once was blind, but the darkness disappeared.
My fancy hairdo has been cut off:
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag2.25.title: Vītasoka

thag2.26.text:
I gave up the five hindrances
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
I took Dhamma as a mirror
for knowing and seeing myself.
I examined this body,
all of it, inside and out.
Internally and externally
my body appeared hollow.
thag2.26.title: Puṇṇamāsa (2nd)

thag2.27.text:
Though a fine thoroughbred may stumble,
it soon stands firm again.
It gains even more urgency,
and draws its load undeterred.
Even so is one accomplished in vision,
a disciple of the Buddha.
Remember me as a thoroughbred,
the Buddha’s bosom son.
thag2.27.title: Nandaka (1st)

thag2.28.text:
Come, Nandaka, let’s go
to visit our preceptor.
We’ll roar our lion’s roar
before the best of Buddhas.
The sage gave us the going forth
out of compassion, so we could realize
the ending of all fetters—
now we have reached that goal.
thag2.28.title: Bharata

thag2.29.text:
This is how the wise roar:
like lions in mountain caves,
heroes, triumphant in battle,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.
I’ve served the Teacher;
I’ve honored the Dhamma and the Saṅgha;
I’m happy and joyful,
because I’ve seen my son free of defilements.
thag2.29.title: Bhāradvāja

thag2.2.text:
You can’t live by fasting,
but food doesn’t lead to peace of heart.
Seeing how this bag of bones is sustained by food,
I wander, seeking.
They know it’s just a swamp,
this homage and veneration in respectable families.
Honor is a subtle dart, hard to extract,
and hard for a reprobate to give up.
thag2.2.title: Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer

thag2.30.text:
I regularly sat close by true persons
and learnt the teaching.
What I learned, I practiced,
the direct route whose objective is freedom from death.
I’ve slain the desire for continued existence,
it won’t be found in me again.
It was not, and it won’t be in me,
and it isn’t found in me now.
thag2.30.title: Kaṇhadinna

thag2.31.text:
When I had gone forth
in the teaching of the Buddha,
while letting go, I rose up;
escaping the sensual realm.
Then, as the supreme one looked on,
my mind was freed.
My freedom is unshakable
with the ending of all fetters.
thag2.31.title: Migasira

thag2.32.text:
Houses are impermanent—
on and on, life after life.
I’ve been searching for the house-builder—
painful is birth again and again.
I’ve seen you, house-builder!
You won’t build a house again.
Your rafters are all broken,
your ridgepole is shattered.
My mind is without boundaries:
in this very life it will dissipate.
thag2.32.title: Sivaka

thag2.33.text:
The perfected one, the Holy One in the world,
the sage is afflicted by winds.
If there’s hot water,
give it to the sage, brahmin.
I wish to bring it to the one
who is esteemed by the estimable,
honored by the honorable,
and venerated by the venerable.
thag2.33.title: Upavāṇa

thag2.34.text:
I’ve seen lay disciples <j>who have memorized discourses,
saying, “Sensual pleasures are impermanent”.
But they’re obsessed with jeweled earrings,
concerned for their partners and children.
To be honest, they don’t know Dhamma,
even though they say <j>“Sensual pleasures are impermanent”.
They don’t have the power to cut their lust,
so they cling to children, wives, and wealth.
thag2.34.title: Isidinna

thag2.35.text:
The heavens rain, the heavens pour,
I’m staying alone in a frightful hole.
But while I’m staying alone in that frightful hole,
I’ve no fear, no dread, no goosebumps.
This is my normal state
while staying alone in a frightful hole:
I’ve no fear,
no dread, no goosebumps.
thag2.35.title: Sambulakaccāna

thag2.37.text:
Night, with her garland of stars,
is not only for sleeping.
For those who know,
this night is really for waking.
Were I to fall from the back of an elephant,
trampled by the tuskers that follow,
better for me to die in battle,
than to live on in defeat.
thag2.37.title: Soṇapoṭiriya

thag2.38.text:
One who’s given up the five sensual stimuli,
so pleasing and delightful,
and who’s left the home life out of faith—
let them make an end to suffering!
I don’t long for death;
I don’t long for life;
I await my time,
aware and mindful.
thag2.38.title: Nisabha

thag2.39.text:
Arranging a robe over my shoulder,
the color of young mango sprouts,
I entered the village for alms
sitting on an elephant’s neck!
But when I dismounted from the elephant,
I was struck with a sense of urgency.
I burned with shame, but then I found peace,
and attained the ending of defilements.
thag2.39.title: Usabha (2nd)

thag2.3.text:
A monkey went up to the little hut
with five doors.
He circles around, knocking
on each door, again and again.
Stand still monkey, don’t run!
Things are different now;
you’ve been caught by wisdom—
you won’t go far.
thag2.3.title: Valliya (2nd)

thag2.40.text:
This chap, “Rag-rice”, he sure is a rag!
Into the vase of freedom from death, <j>polished and overflowing,
sufficient teaching has been poured;
the path to build up absorptions has been laid out.
Don’t nod off, Rag—
I’ll smack your ear!
You know no limit,
nodding off in the midst of the Saṅgha!
thag2.40.title: Kappaṭakura

thag2.41.text:
Oh, the Buddhas! Oh, the Dhammas!
Oh, the accomplishments of the Teacher!
Here a disciple may realize
such a teaching for themselves.
Through countless eons
they obtained substantial forms.
This is their last,
their very final body
in the transmigration through births and deaths;
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag2.41.title: Kassapa the Prince

thag2.42.text:
The young monk
who is devoted to the teaching of the Buddha,
wakeful while others sleep—
his life is not in vain.
So let the wise devote themselves
to faith, ethical behavior,
confidence, and insight into the teaching,
remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.
thag2.42.title: Dhammapāla

thag2.43.text:
Whose faculties have become serene,
like horses tamed by a charioteer?
With conceit and defilements given up,
who is such as envied by even the gods?
My faculties have become serene,
like horses tamed by a charioteer.
With conceit and defilements given up,
I am such as envied by even the gods.
thag2.43.title: Brahmāli

thag2.44.text:
“Your skin is nasty but your heart is good;
Mogharāja, you’re always immersed in samādhi.
But in the nights of winter, so dark and cold,
how will you get by, monk?”
“I’ve heard that all the Magadhans
have an abundance of grain.
I’ll make my bed under a thatched roof,
just like those who live in comfort.”
thag2.44.title: Mogharāja

thag2.45.text:
One should not suspend others from the Saṅgha, <j>nor raise objections against them;
and neither disparage nor raise one’s voice against <j>one who has crossed to the further shore.
One should not praise oneself among the assemblies,
not restless, measured in speech, <j>and true to your vows.
thag2.45.title: Visākhapañcālaputta

thag2.46.text:
The peacocks cry out with their fair crests and tails,
their lovely blue necks and fair faces, <j>their beautiful song and their call.
This broad earth is lush with grass and dew,
and the firmament is full of beautiful clouds.
thag2.46.title: Cūḷaka

thag2.47.text:
The conceited mind, addicted to pleasure,
impales itself on its own stake.
It always goes where
there’s a stake, a chopping board.
I declare you the loser mind!
I declare you the insidious mind!
You’ve found the Teacher so hard to find—
don’t lead me away from the goal.
thag2.47.title: Anūpama

thag2.48.text:
Transmigrating for such a long time,
I’ve cycled through various states of rebirth,
not seeing the noble truths,
a blind, unenlightened person.
But when I became heedful,
transmigrations were mown down.
All states of rebirth are cut off;
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thag2.48.title: Vajjita

thag2.49.text:
Beneath the Bodhi Tree,
bright green and growing,
being mindful, my perception
became one with the Buddha.
It’s been thirty one eons
since I gained that perception;
and it’s due to that perception
that I’ve attained the ending of defilements.
thag2.49.title: Sandhita

thag2.4.text:
My hut on the bank of the Ganges
is made from three palm leaves.
My alms-bowl is a funeral pot,
my robe is cast-off rags.
In my first two rainy seasons
I spoke only one word.
In my third rainy season
the mass of darkness was shattered.
thag2.4.title: Gaṅgātīriya

thag2.5.text:
Even a master of the three knowledges,
undefiled, conqueror of death,
is looked down upon for being unknown
by ignorant fools.
But any individual here
who gets food and drink
is honored by them,
even if they are of bad character.
thag2.5.title: Ajina

thag2.6.text:
When I heard the Teacher
speaking Dhamma,
I wasn’t aware of any doubt
in the all-knowing, unconquered one,
the caravan leader, the great hero,
the most excellent of charioteers.
I have no doubt
in the path or practice.
thag2.6.title: Meḷajina

thag2.8.title: Surādha

thag2.9.text:
Sages sleep at ease
when they’re not bound to women.
For the truth is hard to find among them
and one must always be guarded.
Sensual pleasure, you’ve been slain!
We’re not in your debt any more.
Now we go to extinguishment,
where there is no sorrow.
thag2.9.title: Gotama (1st)

thag20.1.text:
“Living in the wilderness, eating only almsfood,
happy with the scraps in our bowls,
let us tear apart the army of death,
while remaining serene within.
thag20.1.title: Mahāmoggallāna

thag21.1.text:
“Now that I’ve renounced
the lay life for homelessness,
I’m overrun
by the rude thoughts of the Dark One.
thag21.1.title: Vaṅgīsa

thag3.10.text:
In the past you had faith,
today you have none.
What’s yours is yours alone—
I’ve done nothing wrong.
thag3.10.title: Sāṭimattiya

thag3.11.text:
One newly gone forth,
who has left their home out of faith,
should mix with spiritual friends,
who are tireless and pure of livelihood.
thag3.11.title: Upāli

thag3.12.text:
I was, indeed, an astute scholar,
competent to think on the meaning.
The five kinds of sensual stimulation in the world,
so delusory, were my downfall.
thag3.12.title: Uttarapāla

thag3.13.text:
Listen up, all my relatives,
those who have gathered here:
I’ll teach you Dhamma!
Painful is birth again and again.
thag3.13.title: Abhibhūta

thag3.14.text:
Transmigrating, I went to hell,
and to the ghost realm time and again.
Many times I dwelt long
in the animal realm, so full of pain.
thag3.14.title: Gotama (2nd)

thag3.15.text:
Whoever wishes to do afterwards
tasks they should have done before
has lost the causes for happiness,
and afterwards they’re tormented by regrets.
thag3.15.title: Hārita (2nd)

thag3.16.text:
Shunning bad friends,
associate with the supreme individual.
Stick to the advice he gave you,
aspiring to unshakable happiness.
thag3.16.title: Vimala (2nd)

thag3.1.text:
Seeking purity the wrong way,
I served the sacred fire in a grove.
Not knowing the path to purity,
I practiced endless mortification.
thag3.1.title: Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja

thag3.2.title: Paccaya

thag3.4.text:
If you wish to live in happiness,
longing for the ascetic life,
don’t look down on the Saṅgha’s robes,
or its food and drinks.
thag3.4.title: Dhaniya

thag3.5.text:
“It’s too cold, too hot,
too late,” they say.
When the young neglect their work like this,
opportunities pass them by.
thag3.5.title: Mātaṅgaputta

thag3.6.text:
“One of those monks who live in Pāṭaliputta—
such brilliant speakers, and very learned—
stands at the door:
the old man, Khujjasobhita.
thag3.6.title: Khujjasobhita

thag3.7.text:
Anyone among men
who harms other creatures:
that person will fall
both from this world and the next.
thag3.7.title: Vāraṇa

thag3.8.text:
I was the only one in my family
who had faith and wisdom.
It’s good for my relatives that I’m
firm in principle, and ethical.
thag3.8.title: Vassika

thag3.9.text:
“With knobbly knees,
thin and veiny,
eating and drinking but little—
this person’s spirit is undaunted.”
thag3.9.title: Yasoja

thag4.10.text:
“Dhamma surely protects <j>one who practices Dhamma.
The teaching brings happiness when practiced well.
This is the benefit of practicing Dhamma:
one doesn’t go to a bad destination.
thag4.10.title: Dhammika

thag4.11.text:
Well rid of the pack of jackals, <j>mad for the dead,
the lazy frogs croak:
“Today is no time to stray from mountain streams;
Ajakaraṇī is safe, pleasant, and delightful.”
thag4.11.title: Sappaka

thag4.12.text:
Gladly, let this body be broken!
Let this scrap of meat disintegrate!
Let both my legs fall off
at the knees!
thag4.12.title: Mudita

thag4.1.text:
Adorned with jewelry and all dressed up,
with garlands, and sandalwood makeup piled on,
along the main street is a lady—
a dancer dancing as the music plays.
thag4.1.title: Nāgasamāla

thag4.2.text:
Overwhelmed by drowsiness,
I left my dwelling.
Stepping up to the path for walking meditation,
I fell to the ground right there.
thag4.2.title: Bhagu

thag4.4.text:
Curse you mortal frame, you stink!
You’re on Māra’s side, you fester!
O body, you have nine streams
that are flowing all the time.
thag4.4.title: Nandaka (2nd)

thag4.5.title: Jambuka

thag4.6.text:
A great giant, a great hero,
a great light free of defilement.
With the utter ending of all defilements,
the Teacher fears nothing from any quarter.
thag4.6.title: Senaka

thag4.7.title: Sambhūta

thag4.8.text:
I am known as “Fortunate Rāhula”,
because I’m accomplished in both ways:
I am the son of the Buddha,
whose eye sees clearly in all things.
thag4.8.title: Rāhula

thag4.9.text:
Covered over with gold,
surrounded by all her maids,
with my son upon her hip,
my wife came to me.
thag4.9.title: Candana

thag5.10.text:
With fault-finding mind, the simpleton
listens to the victor’s instruction.
They’re as far from the true teaching
as the earth is from the sky.
thag5.10.title: Yasadatta

thag5.11.title: Soṇa of the Sharp Ears

thag5.12.text:
Whatever attentive one, <j>understanding their teacher’s words,
stays with them, their fondness growing;
that astute person is indeed devoted—
knowing the teachings, they’re distinguished.
thag5.12.title: Kosiya

thag5.1.text:
I, a monk, went to a charnel ground
and saw a woman’s body abandoned there,
dumped in a cemetery,
full of worms that devoured.
thag5.1.title: Rājadatta

thag5.2.text:
You should only say what you would do;
you shouldn’t say what you wouldn’t do.
The wise will recognize
one who talks without doing.
thag5.2.title: Subhūta

thag5.4.text:
My mentor helped me to learn,
hoping I would practice those teachings.
Aspiring to freedom from death,
I’ve done what had to be done.
thag5.4.title: Sumana (1st)

thag5.5.text:
Oh so well was the goad
shown to me by my mother,
on hearing whose words,
advised by my mother,
energetic and resolute,
I realized supreme awakening.
thag5.5.title: Vaḍḍha

thag5.6.text:
I used to perform a diverse spectrum of sacrifices;
I served the sacred flame,
imagining, “This is purity.”
I was a blind, ordinary person.
thag5.6.title: Nadīkassapa

thag5.7.text:
Three times a day—
morning, midday, and evening—
I plunged into the water at Gayā
for the Gayā spring festival.
thag5.7.title: Gayākassapa

thag5.8.text:
“Struck by a wind ailment
while dwelling in a forest grove,
you’ve entered a tough place for gathering alms—
how will you get by, monk?”
thag5.8.title: Vakkali

thag5.9.text:
I’ll cage you, mind,
like an elephant in a stockade.
Born of the flesh, that net of the senses,
I won’t urge you to do bad.
thag5.9.title: Vijitasena

thag6.10.text:
I was only seven years old
and had just gone forth
when I overcame the mighty serpent king
with my psychic powers.
thag6.10.title: Sumana (2nd)

thag6.12.text:
Whence anger for one free of anger,
tamed, living justly,
freed by right knowledge,
peaceful and unaffected?
thag6.12.title: Brahmadatta

thag6.14.text:
Like a lurking deer by a trick,
like a fish by a hook,
like a langur by tar—
they trap an ordinary person.
thag6.14.title: Sabbakāmi

thag6.1.text:
Seeing the demonstrations
of the renowned Gotama
was not enough for me to bow to him—
I was blinded by jealousy and conceit.
thag6.1.title: Uruveḷakassapa

thag6.2.text:
“The rice has been harvested
and gathered on the threshing-floor—
but I don’t get any almsfood!
How will I get by?”
thag6.2.title: Tekicchakāri

thag6.3.text:
Whoever has no respect
for their spiritual companions
falls away from the true teaching,
like a fish in a little puddle.
thag6.3.title: Mahānāga

thag6.6.text:
In the twenty-five years
since I went forth,
I have not found peace of mind,
even as long as a finger-snap.
thag6.6.title: Sappadāsa

thag6.7.text:
Get up, Kātiyāna, and sit!
Don’t sleep too much, be wakeful.
Don’t be lazy and let the kinsman of the negligent,
the King of Death, catch you in his trap.
thag6.7.title: Kātiyāna

thag6.8.text:
Emancipating, it leads across,
drying up the root of craving,
and, having cut off the poisonous root, <j>the slaughterhouse,
it leads to quenching.
thag6.8.title: Migajāla

thag6.9.text:
I was drunk with the pride of birth
and wealth and authority.
I wandered about intoxicated
with my own gorgeous body.
thag6.9.title: Jenta, the High Priest’s Son

thag7.1.text:
Adorned with jewelry and all dressed up,
with her garland and her makeup on,
and her feet so brightly rouged:
the courtesan was wearing slippers.
thag7.1.title: Sundarasamudda

thag7.2.text:
Bhaddiya has plucked out craving, root and all,
and in a jungle thicket
on the far side of the Wild Mango Monastery,
he practices absorption; he is truly well-favored.
thag7.2.title: Bhaddiya the Dwarf

thag7.3.text:
I was an only child,
loved by my mother and father.
They had me by practicing
many supplications and observances.
thag7.3.title: Bhadda

thag7.4.text:
I saw the supreme man
walking mindfully in the shade of the terrace,
so I approached,
and bowed to the supreme among men.
thag7.4.title: Sopāka (2nd)

thag7.5.text:
I broke the reeds off with my hands,
made a hut, and stayed there.
That’s how I became known
as “Reed-breaker”.
thag7.5.title: Sarabhaṅga

thag8.1.text:
Don’t get involved in lots of work,
avoid people, and don’t try to acquire things.
If you’re eager and greedy for flavors,
you’ll miss the goal that brings such happiness.
thag8.1.title: Mahākaccāna

thag8.2.text:
Free of anger and acrimony,
free of deceit, and rid of slander;
that’s how such a mendicant
doesn’t grieve after passing away.
thag8.2.title: Sirimitta

thag8.3.text:
Anyone who, having found such a Teacher,
would lose them again,
is like one who, when approached by Lady Luck,
would ward her off with their hands and feet.
thag8.3.title: Mahāpanthaka

thig1.10.text:
Upasamā, cross the flood,
Death’s dominion so hard to pass.
When you have vanquished Māra and his legions,
bear your final body.
thig1.10.title: Upasamā

thig1.11.text:
I’m well freed, so very well freed,
freed from the three things that humped me:
the mortar, the pestle,
and my humpbacked husband.
I’m freed from birth and death;
the leash to existence is eradicated.
thig1.11.title: Muttā (2nd)

thig1.13.text:
Do the Buddha’s bidding,
you won’t regret it.
Having quickly washed your feet,
sit in a discreet place to meditate.
thig1.13.title: Visākhā

thig1.14.text:
Having seen the elements as suffering,
don’t get reborn again.
When you’ve discarded desire for rebirth,
you will live at peace.
thig1.14.title: Sumanā

thig1.15.text:
I was restrained
in body, speech, and mind.
Having plucked out craving, root and all,
I’m cooled and quenched.
thig1.15.title: Uttarā (1st)

thig1.16.title: Sumanā, Who Went Forth Late in Life

thig1.17.text:
I wandered for alms
though feeble, leaning on a staff.
My limbs wobbled
and I fell to the ground right there.
Seeing the danger of the body,
my mind was freed.
thig1.17.title: Dhammā

thig1.18.text:
I gave up my home, my child, my cattle,
and all that I love, and went forth.
And now that I’ve given up desire and hate,
dispelled ignorance,
and plucked out craving, root and all,
I’m at peace, I’m quenched.
thig1.18.title: Saṅghā

thig1.1.title: An Unnamed Nun (1st)

thig1.2.text:
Muttā, be released from your yokes,
like the moon released from the eclipse.
When your mind is released,
enjoy your alms free of debt.
thig1.2.title: Muttā (1st)

thig1.3.text:
Puṇṇā, be filled with good qualities,
like the moon on the fifteenth day.
When your wisdom is full,
shatter the mass of darkness.
thig1.3.title: Puṇṇā

thig1.4.text:
Tissā, train in the trainings—
don’t let your yokes overcome you.
Unyoked from all yokes,
live in the world free of defilements.
thig1.4.title: Tissā

thig1.5.text:
Tissā, apply yourself to good qualities—
don’t let the moment pass you by.
For if you miss your moment,
you’ll grieve when sent to hell.
thig1.5.title: Another Tissā

thig1.6.text:
Dhīrā, touch cessation,
the blissful settling of perception.
Win extinguishment,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
thig1.6.title: Dhīrā

thig1.7.text:
She’s known as Vīrā because of her heroic qualities,
a nun with faculties developed.
She bears her final body,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.
thig1.7.title: Vīrā

thig1.8.text:
Having gone forth in faith,
appreciate your spiritual friends, Mittā.
Develop skillful qualities
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
thig1.8.title: Mittā (1st)

thig10.1.text:
“Pointing out how the world works,
the sages have praised good friendship.
Associating with good friends,
even a fool becomes astute.
thig10.1.title: Kisāgotamī

thig11.1.text:
“The two of us were co-wives,
though we were mother and daughter.
I was struck with a sense of urgency,
so astonishing and hair-raising!
thig11.1.title: Uppalavaṇṇā

thig12.1.text:
“I used to be a water-carrier. Even when it was cold,
I would always plunge into the water,
afraid of my masters’ beatings,
harassed by fear of abuse and anger.
thig12.1.title: Puṇṇikā

thig13.1.text:
My hair was as black as bees,
graced with curly tips;
now old, it has become like hemp bark—
the word of the truthful one is confirmed.
thig13.1.title: Ambapālī

thig13.2.title: Rohinī

thig13.3.text:
“Once I carried a hermit’s staff,
but these days I hunt deer.
My desires have made me unable to cross
from the awful marsh to the far shore.
thig13.3.title: Cāpā

thig13.4.text:
“Before, worthy lady, when feeding
your departed children,
you’d be racked with despair
all day and all night.
thig13.4.title: Sundarī

thig13.5.text:
since I desire to have nothing,
it would not be appropriate
to take back gold and currency,
having already got rid of them.
thig13.5.title: Subhā, the Smith’s Daughter

thig14.1.text:
“What harm have I done to you,
that you stand in my way?
Respectable sir, it’s not proper that a man
should touch a woman gone forth.
thig14.1.title: Subhā of Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

thig15.1.text:
In Pāṭaliputta, the cream of the world,
the city named for a flower,
there were two nuns from the Sakyan clan,
both of them ladies of quality.
thig15.1.title: Isidāsī

thig16.1.text:
In Mantāvatī city, Sumedhā,
the daughter of King Koñca’s chief queen,
was converted by those
who practice the Buddha’s teaching.
thig16.1.title: Sumedhā

thig2.10.text:
Four or five times
I left my dwelling.
I had failed to find peace of heart,
or any control over my mind.
Now it is the eighth night
since craving was eradicated.
Though subject to so many painful things,
I have, through my love of diligence,
reached the ending of craving,
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thig2.10.title: Sāmā

thig2.1.text:
Nandā, see this bag of bones as
diseased, filthy, and rotten.
With mind unified and serene,
meditate on the ugly aspects of the body.
Meditate on the signless,
give up the tendency to conceit;
and when you comprehend conceit,
you will live at peace.
thig2.1.title: Abhirūpanandā

thig2.2.text:
Of the seven awakening factors,
the path for attaining extinguishment,
I have developed them all,
just as the Buddha taught.
For I have seen the Blessed One,
and this bag of bones is my last.
Transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.
thig2.2.title: Jentā

thig2.3.text:
I’m well freed, well freed,
so very well freed from the pestle!
My shameless husband was most certainly a mushroom,
my mortar wafted like an eel.
Greed and hate sizzle and hiss
as I squelch them.
Having gone to the root of a tree,
I meditate happily, thinking, “Oh, what bliss!”
thig2.3.title: Sumaṅgala’s Mother

thig2.4.text:
The price for my services
amounted to the nation of Kāsi.
By setting that price,
the townsfolk made me priceless.
Then, growing disillusioned with my form,
I became dispassionate.
Don’t journey on and on,
transmigrating through rebirths!
I’ve realized the three knowledges,
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thig2.4.title: Aḍḍhakāsi

thig2.5.text:
Even though I’m skinny,
sick, and very feeble,
I climb the mountain,
leaning on a staff.
Having laid down my outer robe,
and overturned my bowl,
propping myself against a rock,
I shattered the mass of darkness.
thig2.5.title: Cittā

thig2.6.text:
Though in pain,
feeble, my youth long gone,
I climb the mountain,
leaning on a staff.
Having laid down my outer robe
and overturned my bowl,
sitting on a rock,
my mind was freed.
I’ve attained the three knowledges,
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thig2.6.title: Mettikā

thig2.8.text:
My dear mother, examine this body,
up from the soles of the feet,
and down from the tips of the hairs,
so impure and foul-smelling.
Meditating like this,
all my lust is eradicated.
The fever of passion is cut off,
I’m cooled and quenched.
thig2.8.title: To Abhayā’s Mother From Her Daughter

thig2.9.text:
Abhayā, the body is fragile,
yet ordinary people are attached to it.
I’ll lay down the body,
aware and mindful.
Though subject to so many painful things,
I have, through my love of diligence,
reached the ending of craving,
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
thig2.9.title: Abhayā

thig3.1.text:
In the twenty-five years
since I went forth,
I don’t know that I had ever found
serenity in my mind.
thig3.1.title: Another Sāmā

thig3.2.text:
Four or five times
I left my dwelling.
I had failed to find peace of heart,
or any control over my mind.
thig3.2.title: Uttamā

thig3.3.text:
Of the seven awakening factors,
the path for attaining extinguishment,
I have developed them all,
just as the Buddha taught.
thig3.3.title: Another Uttamā

thig3.4.text:
Leaving my day’s meditation
on Vulture’s Peak Mountain,
I saw an elephant on the riverbank
having just come up from his bath.
thig3.4.title: Dantikā

thig3.5.text:
“You cry ‘Live, my dear mother!’ in the forest.
Ubbirī, get a hold of yourself!
Eighty-four thousand people,
all named ‘Live’,
have been burnt in this funeral ground:
which one do you grieve for?”
thig3.5.title: Ubbirī

thig3.6.text:
“What’s up with these people in Rājagaha?
They sprawl like they’ve been drinking mead!
They don’t attend on Sukkā
as she teaches the Buddha’s instructions.
thig3.6.title: Sukkā

thig3.7.text:
“There’s no escape in the world,
so what will seclusion do for you?
Enjoy erotic delights;
don’t regret it later.”
thig3.7.title: Selā

thig3.8.text:
“What difference does womanhood make
when the mind is serene,
and knowledge is present
as you rightly discern the Dhamma.
thig3.8.title: Somā

thig4.1.text:
In exactly the same way, Bhaddā daughter of Kapila
is master of the three knowledges, <j>conqueror of death.
She bears her final body,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.
thig4.1.title: Bhaddā Daughter of Kapila

thig5.10.text:
Plowing the fields,
sowing seeds in the ground,
providing for partners and children,
young men acquire wealth.
thig5.10.title: Paṭācārā

thig5.11.text:
“Taking a pestle,
young men pound grain.
Providing for partners and children,
young men acquire wealth.
thig5.11.title: Thirty Nuns

thig5.12.text:
I used to be in a sorry state.
As a childless widow,
bereft of friends or relatives,
I got neither food nor clothes.
thig5.12.title: Candā

thig5.2.text:
Intoxicated by my appearance,
my figure, my beauty, my fame,
and owing to my youth,
I looked down on others.
thig5.2.title: Vimalā, the Former Courtesan

thig5.3.text:
Due to irrational application of mind,
I was racked by desire for pleasures of the senses.
I was restless in the past,
lacking control over my mind.
thig5.3.title: Sīhā

thig5.4.text:
as this is, so is that,
as that is, so is this.
A foul stink wafts from it,
it is the fools’ delight.”
thig5.4.title: Sundarīnandā

thig5.5.text:
In the past I worshiped the sacred flame,
the moon, the sun, and the gods.
Having gone to a river ford,
I plunged into the water.
thig5.5.title: Nanduttarā

thig5.6.text:
Having gone forth in faith
from the lay life to homelessness,
I wandered here and there,
jealous of possessions and honors.
thig5.6.title: Mittākāḷī

thig5.7.text:
Leaving behind my son and my daughter,
my riches and my grain,
I had my hair cut off,
and went forth to homelessness.
thig5.7.title: Sakulā

thig5.8.text:
I gave birth to ten sons
in this form, this bag of bones.
Then, when feeble and old,
I approached a nun.
thig5.8.title: Soṇā

thig5.9.text:
My hair plucked out, covered in mud,
I used to wander wearing just one robe.
I saw fault where there was none,
and was blind to the actual fault.
thig5.9.title: Bhaddā of the Curly Hair

thig6.1.text:
“One whose path you do not know,
not whence they came nor where they went;
though they came from who knows where,
you mourn that being, crying, ‘Oh my son!’
thig6.1.title: Five Hundred Students of Paṭācārā

thig6.2.text:
Struck down with grief for my son,
deranged, out of my mind,
nude, my hair flying,
I wandered here and there.
thig6.2.title: Vāseṭṭhī

thig6.3.text:
“You’re so young and beautiful!
I too am young, just a youth.
Come, Khemā, let us enjoy
the music of a five-piece band.”
thig6.3.title: Khemā

thig6.4.text:
I was adorned with jewelry and all dressed up,
with garlands, and sandalwood makeup piled on,
all covered over with decorations,
and surrounded by my maids.
thig6.4.title: Sujātā

thig6.5.text:
I was born into an eminent family,
affluent and wealthy,
endowed with a beautiful complexion and figure;
Majjha’s true-born daughter.
thig6.5.title: Anopamā

thig6.6.text:
Oh Buddha, my hero: homage to you!
Supreme among all beings,
who released me from suffering,
and many other beings as well.
thig6.6.title: Mahāpajāpati Gotamī

thig6.7.text:
Guttā, you have given up your child,
your wealth, and all that you love.
Foster the goal for which you went forth;
do not fall under the mind’s control.
thig6.7.title: Guttā

thig7.2.text:
“As a nun with developed faculties,
having established mindfulness,
I penetrated that peaceful state,
the blissful stilling of conditions.”
thig7.2.title: Cālā

thig7.3.text:
“A nun with faculties developed,
mindful, seeing clearly,
I penetrated that peaceful state,
which reprobates do not cultivate.”
thig7.3.title: Upacālā

thig8.1.text:
“A nun accomplished in ethics,
her sense faculties well-restrained,
would realize the peaceful state,
so delectable and nutritious.”
thig8.1.title: Sīsūpacālā

thig9.1.text:
“Vaḍḍha, please never ever
get snarled in the world.
My child, do not partake
in suffering again and again.
thig9.1.title: Vaḍḍha’s Mother

kp1.text:
I take refuge in the Buddha,
I take refuge in the Teaching,
I take refuge in the Saṅgha.
kp1.title: The Three Refuges

kp5.text:
“Many gods and humans
have thought about blessings
desiring well-being:
declare the highest blessing.”
kp5.title: Blessings

kp6.text:
Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky;
may beings all be of happy heart,
and listen carefully to what is said.
kp6.title: Gems

kp7.text:
Outside the walls they stand and wait,
at the junctions and the crossroads.
Returning to their former homes
they wait beside the door posts.
kp7.title: Outside the Walls

kp8.text:
free me from rulers if I am slandered,
or from bandits if harassed,
or to release me from debt,
or in case of famine or losses.”
What the world calls savings
get stored away for such reasons.
kp8.title: A Treasure Trove

kp9.text:
content and unburdensome,
unbusied, living lightly,
alert, with senses calmed,
courteous, not fawning on families.
kp9.title: The Discourse on Love

snp1.10.text:
“What’s a person’s best wealth?
What brings happiness when practiced well?
What’s the sweetest taste of all?
The one they say has the best life: how do they live?”
snp1.10.title: With Āḷavaka

snp1.11.text:
Walking and standing,
sitting and lying down,
extending and contracting the limbs:
these are the movements of the body.
snp1.11.title: Victory Over Desire for the Body

snp1.12.text:
Peril stems from intimacy,
dust comes from an abode.
Freedom from abode and intimacy:
that is the sage’s vision.
snp1.12.title: The Sage

snp1.1.text:
They’ve cut off greed entirely,
like a lotus plucked flower and stalk.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
snp1.1.title: The Serpent

snp1.2.text:
“I’ve boiled my rice and drawn my milk,”
“I stay with my family along the bank of the Mahī.
My hut is roofed, my sacred fire kindled:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
snp1.2.title: The Wealthy Rancher

snp1.3.text:
As a spreading bamboo gets entangled,
so does concern for partners and children.
Like a bamboo shoot unobstructed,
live alone like a horned rhino.
snp1.3.title: The Horned Rhino

snp1.4.text:
“You claim to be a farmer,
but I don’t see you farming.
Tell me your farming when asked,
so I can recognize your farming.”
snp1.4.title: With Bhāradvāja the Farmer

snp1.5.text:
“I ask the sage abounding in wisdom,”
“the Buddha, master of the teaching, free of craving,
best of men, excellent charioteer, please tell me this:
how many ascetics are there in the world?”
snp1.5.title: With Cunda

snp1.6.text:
“We ask Gotama
about a man’s downfall.
We have come to ask you, sir:
what leads to downfall?”
snp1.6.title: Downfalls

snp1.7.text:
“Irritable and acrimonious,
wicked and offensive,
a man deficient in view, deceitful:
know him as a lowlife.
snp1.7.title: The Lowlife

snp1.9.text:
“Today is the fifteenth day sabbath,”
“a holy night is at hand.
Come now, let us see Gotama,
the Teacher of peerless name.”
snp1.9.title: With Hemavata

snp2.10.text:
Get up and meditate!
What’s the point in your sleeping?
How can the afflicted slumber
when inflicted by an arrow strike?
snp2.10.title: Get Up!

snp2.11.text:
“Does familiarity breed contempt,
even for the man of wisdom?
Do you honor he who holds aloft
the torch for all humanity?”
snp2.11.title: With Rāhula

snp2.12.text:
“I ask the Teacher unrivaled in wisdom,
who has cut off all doubts in this very life:
a monk has died at Āḷavī’s premier shrine,
who was well-known, famous, and quenched.
snp2.12.title: Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa

snp2.13.text:
“I ask the sage abounding in wisdom—
crossed-over, gone beyond, quenched, steadfast:
when a mendicant has left home, <j>casting aside sensuality,
what’s the right way to wander the world?”
snp2.13.title: The Right Way to Wander

snp2.14.text:
“I ask you, Gotama, whose wisdom is vast:
what does one do to become a good disciple,
both one who has left the home,
and the lay followers staying at home?
snp2.14.title: With Dhammika

snp2.2.text:
“The good eat properly obtained
millet, wild grains, broomcorn,
greens, tubers, and grapes.
They don’t lie to get what they want.
snp2.2.title: Putrefaction

snp2.3.text:
Flouting conscience, loathing it,
saying “I’m on your side”,
but not following up in deeds—
know they’re not on your side.
snp2.3.title: Conscientious Companionship

snp2.5.title: With Spiky

snp2.6.text:
A mendicant who loves to quarrel,
wrapped in delusion,
doesn’t even know what’s been explained
in the Dhamma taught by the Buddha.
snp2.6.title: A Righteous Life

snp2.7.text:
“The ancient seers used to be
restrained and austere.
Having given up the five sensual stimuli,
they lived for their own true good.
snp2.7.title: Brahmanical Principles

snp2.8.text:
If you would learn the teaching from someone,
honor them as the gods honor Indra.
Then they will have confidence in you,
and being learned, they reveal the teaching.
snp2.8.title: The Boat

snp2.9.text:
“With what morality, what conduct,
fostering what deeds,
would a person lay the foundations right,
and reach the highest goal?”
snp2.9.title: What Morality?

snp3.10.text:
“A person is born
with an axe in their mouth.
A fool cuts themselves with it
when they say bad words.
snp3.10.title: With Kokālika

snp3.11.text:
The seer Asita in his daily meditation
saw the bright-clad gods of the host of Thirty
and their lord Sakka joyfully celebrating,
waving streamers in exuberant exaltation.
snp3.11.title: About Nālaka

snp3.12.text:
They’re endowed with the heart’s release,
as well as the release by wisdom.
Able to make an end,
they don’t continue to be reborn and grow old.”
snp3.12.title: Contemplating Pairs

snp3.1.text:
“I shall extol going forth
with the example of the Clear-eyed One,
the course of inquiry that led to
his choice to go forth.
snp3.1.title: Going Forth

snp3.2.text:
“During my time of resolute striving
back on the bank of the Nerañjara River,
I was meditating very hard
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
snp3.2.title: Striving

snp3.3.title: Well-Spoken Words

snp3.4.text:
“I am no brahmin, nor am I a ruler,
nor peasant nor anything else.
Fully understanding the clan of ordinary people,
I wander in the world owning nothing, reflective.
snp3.4.title: With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake

snp3.5.text:
“I ask the bountiful Gotama,”
“wearing an ochre robe, wandering homeless.
Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity
makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit,
giving food and drink to others here:
how is their offering purified?”
snp3.5.title: With Māgha

snp3.6.text:
“I’ve come full of  doubts and uncertainties,”
“wishing to ask some questions.
Please solve them for me.
Answer my questions in turn, <j>in accordance with the truth.”
snp3.6.title: With Sabhiya

snp3.8.text:
Unforeseen and unknown
is the extent of this mortal life—
hard and short
and bound to pain.
snp3.8.title: The Dart

snp3.9.text:
“We’re both authorized masters
of the three Vedas.
I’m a student of Pokkharasāti,
and he of Tārukkha.
snp3.9.title: With Vāseṭṭha

snp4.10.text:
“Seeing how, behaving how,
is one said to be at peace?
When asked, Gotama, please tell me
about the ultimate person.”
snp4.10.title: Before the Breakup

snp4.11.text:
“Quarrels and disputes come from what we hold dear,
as do lamentation and sorrow, stinginess,
conceit and arrogance.
Quarrels and disputes are linked to stinginess,
and when disputes have arisen there is slander.”
snp4.11.title: Quarrels and Disputes

snp4.12.text:
“Each maintaining their own view,
those who are skilled disagree, arguing:
‘Whoever sees it this way <j>understands the teaching;
those who reject this are inadequate.’
snp4.12.title: The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle

snp4.13.text:
“Regarding those who maintain their own view,
disputing that, ‘This is the only truth’:
are all of them subject only to criticism,
or do some also win praise for that?”
snp4.13.title: The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle

snp4.14.text:
“Great seer, I ask you, the Kinsman of the Sun,
about seclusion and the state of peace.
How, having seen, is a mendicant extinguished,
not grasping anything in this world?”
snp4.14.title: Speedy

snp4.15.text:
Peril stems from those who take up arms—
just look how people conflict!
I shall extol how I came to be
